newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Drunk, hungry or mad-is your dog insured?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Drunk, hungry or mad-is your dog insured?.

text.p: Man's best friend? Sometimes.
Owning a dog can bring calamities as well as laughs and the insurance industry often picks up the bill.
There are more than 6.5 million dogs in Britain, giving a lot of scope for doggy disasters.

A dog's greatest enemy is often itself. Gargantuan appetites and inquisitive natures combine to produce no end of accidents. With ballooning vet bills, some owners are looking to specialist insurance firms for protection against their pets.
"The cost of treatment has increased. That has been the driving force behind the growth of pet insurance," said John McMurray, managing director of Dog Breeders' Insurance.
McMurray insures cats and horses as well, but dogs are the most frequent customers, accounting for 80 percent of claims.
"Dogs tend to do sillier things. They're more mischievous whereas cats are more streetwise," McMurray said.
DOGS IN THE DOLDRUMS
Dogs and food often lead to trouble.
Springer had a heavy Christmas after he guzzled a fruit cake laced with brandy. His owners arrived home to find him rolling around on the floor drunk, his stomach the size of a football.

Springer spent the evening having his stomach pumped and felt fragile for the next five days. But his insurance company, Petplan, paid the bill for 98 pounds ($160) which went some way to easing his hangover.
Glove, a boxer, vomited and collapsed after chomping his way through a sleeping bag. Pet Protect paid his 100 pounds medical fee and Glove recovered.

With the cost of looking after a dog averaging around 720 pounds a year, unforseen vet bills are an unwelcome extra cost. The RSPCA (Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals) recommends that every owner insures their animal.

"A lot of the prosecutions the RSPCA takes for cruelty are actually caused by neglect, which is often not taking animals to the vet when it needs to go. Very often the excuse that's given is we couldn't afford it," said spokeswoman Jo Crozier.

When labrador Chloe swallowed a razor blade, Pet Protect paid 100 pounds for it to be removed. Chloe was put under general anaesthetic while the blade was carefully dragged from her stomach through her throat using a fibre-optic endoscope.
But one Irish wolfhound's escapades really take the biscuit.

Before his first birthday, Flynn had munched through four doggie beds, two baby mattresses, a garden hose, bed linen, knickers, socks, T-shirts, leggings, shoes, a dustpan and brush, a watering can, cigarettes, and part of a picket fence.
Three separate binges involving a tea towel, a hand towel, and the entire contents of a dustbin, resulted in trips to the vet for vomit-inducing injections.
But Flynn can shrug off jokes about having half a brain -- they are true. A scan showed his brain had not formed properly.

Since this diagnosis, Flynn has paid his vet yet another visit. He leapt from an upstairs window at his home, miraculously surviving a 15 foot (4-1/2 metre) drop onto crazy-paving with no more than a nasty cut in his back leg.
Undeterred, Flynn continued to pad over to the same window. His owner installed a baby gate to curb his flying tendencies.
He ate that as well.
Flynn's mishaps have resulted in more than 1,000 pounds of vet's bills, making him one of Petplan's more expensive customers.
But dogs can be a danger to others as well as themselves. Non-specialist insurance companies are bombarded with claims for damage caused by accident-prone pooches.
DANGEROUS DOGS
A Hertfordshire man left Digby in the car while he popped into a shop. When he emerged, the car and Digby had disappeared. Passers-by reported seeing a large dog at the wheel.
Digby had released the hand-brake but his skills did not stretch to driving and he crashed into a tree, causing 2,000 pounds worth of damage, which Eagle Star paid.
A labrador was briefly tied to a golf trolley in the car park while his owner nipped into the club house.

Startled by a car back-firing, the terrified dog charged around the car park with the trolley, denting wings and smashing headlights to the tune of more than 2,000 pounds. His owner sent the bill to Cornhill Insurance.
DOGS TO THE RESCUE
But it's unfair to portray all dogs as liabilities.
Star's neighbours thought it strange that the normally well-behaved dog was barking furiously from a bedroom window -- until they saw smoke and flames coming from the roof.
Star was unconscious when the paramedics arrived but they managed to clear the smoke and grime from her lungs using a suction machine, saving her life.
After such heroics, Petplan could not refuse her claim of 207 pounds towards treatment.
